section.title: Everlasting Salvation for Zion
section.sectionRationale: This long movement gathers up nearly every thread of the Book of Comfort, Abraham and Sarah as the rock Israel was cut from, the Servant's righteousness as a light to the nations, the awakened arm of the LORD that once split the sea, the cup of wrath finally removed from Zion's hand, and the herald whose feet are beautiful because he announces that God reigns. It ends with a sober command to leave Babylon and carry the LORD's vessels home. It stands as the long crescendo just before the fourth Servant Song.
section.thesis: The LORD who called Abraham from nothing and dried up the sea for the redeemed to cross will again bare His holy arm to comfort Zion, remove the cup of His fury, and send good news of salvation to the ends of the earth, so His people can wake up, put on strength, and leave captivity behind.
section.frameNote: Eight movements: look to Abraham and Sarah; the law and light to the nations; awake, O arm of the LORD; I, even I, am He who comforts you; awake, awake, Jerusalem, the cup removed; awake, awake, clothe yourself, O Zion; how beautiful are the feet who bring good news; and depart, depart, go out from there.

units.label: Look to the rock you were cut from
units.note: Abraham and Sarah, the pattern of God's multiplying grace

verses.text: “Listen to Me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: Look to the rock from which you were cut, and to the quarry from which you were hewn.
Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth. When I called him, he was but one; then I blessed him and multiplied him.

For the LORD will comfort Zion and will look with compassion on all her ruins; He will make her wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD. Joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and melodious song.

units.label: A law and a light to the nations

verses.text: Pay attention to Me, My people, and listen to Me, My nation; for a law will go out from Me, and My justice will become a light to the nations; I will bring it about quickly.
My righteousness draws near, My salvation is on the way, and My arms will bring justice to the nations. The islands will look for Me and wait in hope for My arm.

Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth below; for the heavens will vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment, and its people will die like gnats. But My salvation will last forever, and My righteousness will never fail.
Listen to Me, you who know what is right, you people with My law in your hearts: Do not fear the scorn of men; do not be broken by their insults.
For the moth will devour them like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool. But My righteousness will last forever, My salvation through all generations.”

units.label: Awake, O arm of the LORD
units.note: the God who cut Rahab and dried the sea

verses.text: Awake, awake, put on strength, O {{zeroa|arm}} of the LORD. Wake up as in days past, as in generations of old. Was it not You who cut {{rahab|Rahab}} to pieces, who pierced through the dragon?
Was it not You who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over?
So the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee.

units.label: I, even I, am He who comforts you

verses.text: “I, even I, am He who comforts you. Why should you be afraid of mortal man, of a son of man who withers like grass?

But you have forgotten the LORD, your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth. You live in terror all day long because of the fury of the oppressor who is bent on destruction. But where is the fury of the oppressor?
The captive will soon be freed; he will not die in the dungeon, and his bread will not be lacking.
For I am the LORD your God who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar, the LORD of Hosts is His name.
I have put My words in your mouth, and covered you with the shadow of My hand, to establish the heavens, to found the earth, and to say to Zion, ‘You are My people.’”
Awake, awake! Rise up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury; you who have drained the goblet to the dregs, the cup that makes men stagger.
Among all the sons she bore, there is no one to guide her; among all the sons she brought up, there is no one to take her hand.
These pairs have befallen you: devastation and destruction, famine and sword. Who will grieve for you? Who can comfort you?
Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street, like an antelope in a net. They are full of the wrath of the LORD, the rebuke of your God.
Therefore now hear this, you afflicted one, drunken, but not with wine.
Thus says your Lord, the LORD, even your God, who defends His people: “See, I have removed from your hand the cup of staggering. From that goblet, the cup of My fury, you will never drink again.
I will place it in the hands of your tormentors, who told you: ‘Lie down, so we can walk over you,’ so that you made your back like the ground, like a street to be traversed.”

units.label: Awake, awake, clothe yourself, O Zion
units.note: sold for nothing, redeemed without money

verses.text: Awake, awake, clothe yourself with strength, O Zion! Put on your garments of splendor, O Jerusalem, holy city! For the uncircumcised and unclean will no longer enter you.
Shake off your dust! Rise up and sit on your throne, O Jerusalem. Remove the chains from your neck, O captive Daughter of Zion.
For this is what the LORD says: “You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed.”
For this is what the Lord GOD says: “At first My people went down to Egypt to live, then Assyria oppressed them without cause.
And now what have I here? declares the LORD. For My people have been taken without cause; those who rule them taunt, declares the LORD, and My name is blasphemed continually all day long.
Therefore My people will know My name; therefore they will know on that day that I am He who speaks. Here I am!”

units.label: How beautiful are the feet
units.note: good news, peace, salvation, your God reigns

verses.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring {{besorah|good news}}, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation, who say to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
Listen! Your watchmen lift up their voices, together they shout for joy. For every eye will see when the LORD returns to Zion.
Break forth in joy, sing together, O ruins of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted His people; He has redeemed Jerusalem.
The LORD has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations; all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God.

units.label: Depart, depart, go out from there
units.note: carry the vessels of the LORD, purified

verses.text: Depart, depart, go out from there! Touch no unclean thing; come out from it, purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD.
For you will not leave in a hurry nor flee in haste, for the LORD goes before you, and the God of Israel is your rear guard.

zeroa.gloss: Arm, the picture of God's active, saving strength. Awake, O arm of the LORD calls on the same power that split the sea at the exodus to act again; the same phrase, God's arm bared, returns in 52:10 and 53:1, tying creation, exodus, and the Servant's suffering together as one unfolding display of divine strength.

rahab.gloss: A poetic name for a sea monster or the chaos of the deep, sometimes used for Egypt itself. To cut Rahab to pieces recalls both God's victory over chaos at creation and His defeat of Egypt at the exodus, one image doing double duty as cosmic and historical deliverance.

besorah.gloss: Good news, glad tidings, the root behind the New Testament word for gospel. The herald's beautiful feet bring besorah that God reigns and has redeemed His people; Paul quotes this verse directly in Romans 10:15 of those who preach the good news of Christ.

basic.context: This long section gathers the Book of Comfort's key promises before the climactic fourth Servant Song. Israel in exile is told to remember Abraham, to trust the arm that split the sea, and to know that the cup of God's wrath, which she has drained to the dregs, will finally be removed and placed instead in the hands of her tormentors.
basic.hermeneutics: The repeated cry awake, awake structures the whole passage, first summoning God's arm to act, then Jerusalem to rise from her stupor, then Zion to clothe herself for restoration. It is prophetic poetry announcing a real, historical return from Babylon that also reaches, in language too large for Babylon alone, toward final salvation.
basic.originalLanguages: The zeroa, arm, of the LORD ties creation's defeat of Rahab, the exodus through the sea, and the coming salvation into a single continuous act of divine strength. And the herald's feet are beautiful because they carry besorah, good news, the very word behind gospel, that God reigns.
basic.typology: The arm of the LORD bared for all the nations to see anticipates the arm of the LORD revealed in the Suffering Servant of chapter 53. The herald whose feet are beautiful anticipates every gospel messenger, and supremely Christ Himself, the good news in person.
basic.christ: Paul quotes 52:7 directly in Romans 10:15 of gospel preachers, and applies the phrase how beautiful are the feet to the spread of the good news about Jesus. The bared arm of the LORD in 52:10 leads directly into 53:1, who has believed our message, and to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed, showing that the ultimate unveiling of God's saving arm is the crucified and risen Christ.
basic.god: God is the covenant-keeping Creator who called one man, Abraham, and multiplied him into a people; He is also the Judge who poured out real wrath on real sin, yet He is the Redeemer who removes that same cup from His people's hand and hands it instead to their oppressors, precisely and only because of what the coming Servant will bear.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 10:15 quotes Isaiah 52:7 of gospel messengers. Galatians 3:6-9 appeals to Abraham as father of all who believe. Isaiah 53:1 continues directly from 52:10 with who has believed our message. Revelation 18 echoes the cup of God's fury given finally to Babylon.
basic.oneStory: From Abraham the one, to the arm that split the sea, to the cup of wrath finally removed and carried instead by another, the whole passage is one long rehearsal of the story the Bible tells everywhere: God saves a helpless, guilty people by His own strength, and sends good news of it running to the ends of the earth.

context.literary:
The whole of Isaiah 51:1 to 52:12 is held together by a rhythm of summons. It begins with three calls to listen, each opening 'Listen to Me' or 'Pay attention to Me', at 51:1, 51:4 and 51:7, and each addressed to a slightly different audience: those who pursue righteousness, the nation as a whole, and those with the law in their hearts. The LORD speaks, and the people are asked only to hear. Then the voice reverses. The people, or the prophet on their behalf, cry out in 51:9, 'Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD.' The LORD answers in 51:12 with the doubled 'I, even I, am He who comforts you.' He then turns the same summons upon Jerusalem in 51:17, 'Awake, awake! Rise up,' and upon Zion in 52:1, 'Awake, awake, clothe yourself.' The same verb, from the root meaning to rouse oneself, carries through all three, so the one who is asked to wake is first God's arm and then God's people.

The movement ends with a fourth doubled imperative that is the opposite of waking in place: 'Depart, depart, go out from there,' 52:11. So the section is built from listening, then waking, then leaving. It is a liturgy of return, in which every command is made possible by what comes just before it.

Notice how the poem keeps pairing the cosmic with the intimate. The same mouth that talks of the heavens vanishing like smoke in 51:6 also says 'I have put My words in your mouth, and covered you with the shadow of My hand', 51:16. The same power that cut Rahab to pieces is the power that promises to defend a staggering Jerusalem. This is not an accident of style. Isaiah wants the exiles to see that the God of creation and the God of their small, shaky lives are the same God.

The central panel, 51:17 to 23, is a reversal. The cup of fury that Jerusalem drained is taken from her hand and put into her tormentors' hands. The poem then flips again with the glad news that reaches the mountains in 52:7, where the reader meets a runner on the heights shouting a very short sentence in the Hebrew, 'Your God reigns'. Everything before it was preparation for that cry, and everything after it, the watchmen, the ruins singing, the bared arm, unfolds from it.
context.historical:
The setting is the last decades of the exile, as the Persian king Cyrus rose and Babylon grew vulnerable. Isaiah has already named Cyrus as the LORD's shepherd and anointed, Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1, and this section pushes the exiles to act on their hope. Cyrus's decree in 538 BC allowed the Jews to go home and even returned the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had carried off, Ezra 1:7 and 8. That detail lies behind the command of 52:11, 'you who carry the vessels of the LORD.' The vessels are literal, and the people carrying them take on a priestly role, as those who bring back what belongs to the temple.

The comparison to Abraham in 51:1 and 2 has special weight for exiles. They were few, and Abraham had been one. The nation had shrunk to a remnant in a foreign land, much like the single, childless old man whom God called and then multiplied, and Isaiah invites them to treat their smallness as a reason for hope rather than despair. Hebrews 11:11 and 12 later makes the same point about Sarah and the stars.

Verse 3 promises that Zion's ruins will be made like Eden. A returning generation would have found Jerusalem in rubble, and the promise to turn desert into a garden was one that Ezekiel also made, Ezekiel 36:35. The word picture is of a land wasted by war and neglect, brought back to the original design.

The 'cup of fury' belongs to a familiar image in Israel's prophets, where God hands a cup to the nations and they drink and stagger, Jeremiah 25:15 to 17 and Psalm 75:8. Jerusalem has drunk it to the dregs. The picture of tormentors saying 'Lie down, so we can walk over you' in 51:23 describes the humiliation of the conquered, with their backs made a road. The reversal promised here, that the cup goes to Babylon, matches Jeremiah 51:6 and what later Scripture says about Babylon's own fall, Revelation 14:8.

The Egypt and Assyria of 52:4 stand for the two ends of Israel's history of oppression: a sojourn that became slavery, and an empire that attacked without reason. Isaiah's point is that the LORD has been through this before and has acted, and that the blasphemy of His name among the nations, 52:5, is a cost He takes personally. Paul quotes the Greek of this verse in Romans 2:24.
context.canonical:
This is a section that other Scripture keeps picking up. Its opening, 'Look to Abraham your father', depends on Genesis 12:1 to 3, where the LORD calls one man and promises that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him, and on Genesis 15:5, where the stars are counted. Paul uses Abraham as the pattern of faith in Galatians 3:6 to 9 and Romans 4:16 and 17, and Hebrews 11 brings Sarah in by name.

The 'arm of the LORD' appears across the second half of Isaiah as a repeated signature. It comes in 40:10, in 51:5 and 51:9, in 52:10, in 53:1 and in 63:5, where the arm 'brought Me salvation.' The section here is the hinge at which the arm moves from being a figure of rescue to being revealed in a person, because within a few verses of 52:10 the text asks 'to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?' John quotes the question in John 12:38 and Paul in Romans 10:16.

The cup is another thread. It runs from Psalm 75:8 and Jeremiah 25:15 to 17 through this chapter to Gethsemane, where Jesus prays 'let this cup pass from Me', Matthew 26:39, and tells Peter, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?', John 18:11. Revelation pours it out on Babylon, Revelation 14:8 and 18:6.

Isaiah 52:7 is quoted in Romans 10:15 to explain why preachers must be sent, and the footnote to the BSB notes that 52:11 is cited in 2 Corinthians 6:17 and that the Septuagint of 52:5 is cited in Romans 2:24. The call 'Come out of her, My people' in Revelation 18:4 echoes the command to leave Babylon, which also recalls Jeremiah 51:6. The returning, singing crowd of 51:11 is word for word the promise of Isaiah 35:10, so the two texts sit as bookends to the same vision.

Finally the 'light to the nations' of 51:4, which echoes 42:6 and 49:6, is applied to Jesus by Simeon in Luke 2:32 and to the mission of the apostles by Paul and Barnabas in Acts 13:47.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted a discouraged people to do three things in order: remember, wake and leave. The remembering is deliberate. Abraham, the sea and the first creation are all about God's power to make something from nothing, and the exiles are invited to look back so that they can look forward. They are not asked to feel nothing about their loss; the section freely describes the staggering, famished, fainting sons of Jerusalem. The remembering is aimed at the one fear that held them back, which was fear of men, 51:7 and 12, whose threats Isaiah says are as brittle as grass and moth-eaten cloth.

The waking is a change of posture. The exiles had grown used to a stooped, sedated life under Babylon, and the poem calls Jerusalem to shake off the dust and take her seat as a queen, 52:2. It is the opposite of what a conquered city expects to hear. The author means them to hear that their status has changed before their circumstances have.

The leaving is practical. After the promises Isaiah gives instructions. They are to go out, and to go out clean, carrying the LORD's vessels. The calm of 52:12, that they will not leave in haste because the LORD goes before and behind, is meant to counter a decision made out of panic. He wanted the exiles to move at God's call, not at the pace of their fear, and to trust that the way home was guarded on both sides.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The promises here are specific to a people in exile and to a time when God was about to act through Cyrus. They describe what God will do and commands His people to respond. They do not promise that every ruin will be made like Eden in the believer's lifetime, nor that every oppressor will be dealt with quickly. The sweeping images of 51:3 and 51:11 look to the final restoration, which the New Testament places at the end, Revelation 21:1 to 5.

What is prescribed is clear. Listen. Look to the rock and the quarry. Do not fear the scorn of men. Wake and put on strength. Leave Babylon and touch no unclean thing. Paul applies the last of these directly to the church, 2 Corinthians 6:17, and John does the same, Revelation 18:4. In each case the command is not a call to withdraw from the world but to refuse to share in what stands under judgment.

It also helps to notice what is not commanded. Nobody is told to take up arms against Babylon, and the exiles are not asked to bring about their own rescue. They are asked to trust and to go when the moment comes. The lesson for readers is to resist reading the passage as a recipe for self-confidence, since the strength they are told to put on in 52:1 belongs to Zion only because the LORD has already acted.

debates.question: Who is speaking in Isaiah 51:9 to 11, and to whom?

views.label: The prophet, or the faithful remnant, in prayer to the LORD
views.case: The verses are addressed to the 'arm of the LORD' and use the second person, 'Was it not You who cut Rahab to pieces?' It reads as a prayer of lament, asking the LORD to act again as He did at the exodus. The LORD answers in verse 12 with 'I, even I, am He who comforts you', so the section works as a call and response.

views.label: The LORD's own voice calling on His power to act
views.case: A smaller number of readers take the summons as a poetic address spoken within the divine speech, so that the 'arm' is an agent summoned to action. The arm of the LORD is elsewhere almost personified, as in 53:1.

debates.bearing: Either way the content is the same: the exodus is held up as the pattern for a coming deliverance, and the answer to the prayer is God's own promise of comfort. The poem leaves open whether the arm is merely a figure or something more, and Isaiah 53:1 will push it toward a person.

debates.question: How far does the fulfilment of this passage reach?

views.label: The return from Babylon in the sixth century BC
views.case: The commands to leave, to carry the vessels and to depart without haste match the return under Cyrus, Ezra 1:7 and 8. The language of ruins and Eden fits the rebuilding of Jerusalem, as in Ezekiel 36:35.

views.label: The final salvation through Christ and the new creation
views.case: Some images are too large for the return alone. The heavens vanish and the earth wears out in 51:6, sorrow and sighing flee in 51:11, the unclean never again enter Jerusalem in 52:1, and all the ends of the earth see God's salvation in 52:10. Paul applies 52:7 to gospel preaching and the Revelation echoes it of the end.

views.label: A pattern that is fulfilled in stages
views.case: Many readers see the return from Babylon as a first stage in a pattern completed in Christ and consummated at the end. The returnees went home, but the nations did not see the LORD's salvation, and the people did not yet live in lasting peace.

debates.bearing: The third view fits best how the New Testament uses the passage. It treats the Babylonian return as real and as a down payment, and treats Christ's work as the event that opens the larger fulfilment, which will be completed when He returns.

study.originalLanguages:
The doubled command 'Awake, awake' in 51:9, 51:17 and 52:1 comes from one root meaning to rouse oneself. In 51:9 the form is a plain imperative, and in 51:17 it is the reflexive stem, which has a sense of rousing oneself. The change matters. The arm of the LORD is called to wake and act; Jerusalem is called to wake herself. In 50:4 the same root described the Servant's ear being awakened each morning. The Servant therefore listens, and then the people are woken to follow.

In 51:12 the LORD says 'I, even I, am He who comforts you.' The doubling of the pronoun is one of Isaiah's signatures. The same emphatic pair appears in 43:25, 'I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions', and the claim in 41:4, 'I am He'. When He comforts, He insists that He Himself, not an agent or substitute, is the one who comforts. The verb comfort is the opposite of the grief of 51:19, where the question is 'Who can comfort you?' The BSB footnote notes that the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Vulgate read 'Who can comfort you?' while the traditional Hebrew text reads 'How can I comfort you?' The textual difference changes the grammar of the line, and the sense of the passage is unaffected: no one can comfort her, and so God will.

The name 'Rahab' in 51:9 sits beside 'the dragon', a word that also names the great monster of Egypt in Ezekiel 29:3. Rahab is cut to pieces in Job 26:12 and crushed in Psalm 89:10. Isaiah uses it for chaos and for Egypt together, so that one image of conquest covers both the sea monster of creation and the sea of the exodus. The next line makes the link explicit, with the sea dried up and a road made in the depths 'for the redeemed to cross over', 51:10.

The 'cup' of 51:17 and 51:22 is called the cup of staggering, and the 'dregs' are the last drops that hold the strongest dose. The picture is of a drinker who has been made to finish the whole thing. The verb in 51:22 'I have removed' is perfect in form, a sure thing, while the promise that she will never drink again is about the future.

The herald of 52:7 is a participle, one who brings news, and the same root appears in 40:9, 'herald of good news'. The Septuagint renders it with a Greek verb from which we get 'evangelise', and Paul uses it in Romans 10:15. The four phrases, good news, peace, good tidings and salvation, pile up one meaning on another until the message is stated in the briefest of sentences in 52:7: 'Your God reigns.' The announcement is not a general truth. It is something happening on the mountains, now.

The word translated 'haste' in 52:12 is the one used of the first Passover meal, 'eat in haste', Exodus 12:11, and of the day Israel left Egypt, Deuteronomy 16:3. Isaiah is describing a second exodus that will differ from the first on exactly this point: the people will not flee. The 'rear guard' recalls the pillar of cloud that moved behind Israel in Exodus 14:19 and 20.

typology.type: Abraham and Sarah, the one who became many, Isaiah 51:1 and 2
typology.fulfillment: A single childless couple, 'but one', becomes a multitude. The pattern reaches into the New Testament in two directions. Hebrews 11:11 and 12 calls Sarah's conception an act of faith, and Paul argues that Abraham is the father of all who believe, Romans 4:16 and 17. In Christ the many become the family of the one Seed, Galatians 3:16 and 3:29. The correspondence strengthens: what God did through a barren womb He does through a crucified and risen Man, by whom a multitude from every nation is counted among Abraham's offspring. The type falls short because Abraham's family came by birth, while Christ's comes by faith and new birth.

typology.type: The sea crossing and the road for the redeemed, Isaiah 51:9 and 10
typology.fulfillment: The exodus is the pattern for every later rescue, and Isaiah calls it up as the template for a second one. Luke says that Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus on the mountain about the 'departure' He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31, a word that is the same as 'exodus'. The cross and resurrection become the new passage through the waters. The pattern extends to baptism, 1 Corinthians 10:1 and 2, and to the redeemed crossing at the end, Revelation 15:2 to 3. The type falls short because the first exodus delivered a people from an earthly tyrant, whereas Christ delivers from sin and death.

typology.type: The cup of wrath removed, Isaiah 51:17 to 22
typology.fulfillment: Jerusalem drained the cup and the LORD took it from her hand. In the Gospels Jesus is the one who takes it. He asks that the cup might pass and then says 'Not as I will, but as You will', Matthew 26:39, and tells Peter that He must drink what the Father has given Him, John 18:11. The cup of 51:22 is not poured out again on His people, since He has drunk it for them. The type is not a simple swap: Isaiah gives the cup to the oppressors, while the New Testament says Christ takes it first, and at the end the cup is still given to Babylon, Revelation 14:8 and 18:6.

typology.type: The herald on the mountains, Isaiah 52:7
typology.fulfillment: The runner who announces that God reigns is a type of everyone who carries the news. Paul quotes the verse of the preachers of the gospel, Romans 10:15, and Jesus opens His ministry with the message that the kingdom of God is near, Mark 1:14 and 15. Ephesians 6:15 even calls the gospel a 'gospel of peace' for the feet. The escalation is that the herald in Isaiah announces a rescue still to come, while the heralds of the New Testament announce one that has been accomplished at the cross and in the resurrection. The type falls short because the herald is only the messenger, but Jesus is also the message, Mark 1:15.

typology.type: The departure from Babylon with the vessels, Isaiah 52:11 and 12
typology.fulfillment: The people who carry the LORD's vessels are to be clean. Paul takes the command and applies it to the church, 2 Corinthians 6:17, and John hears the same summons at the fall of the last Babylon, Revelation 18:4. The pattern is a movement out of a compromised world towards God's own presence with a guard before and behind. It is fulfilled in Christ's people, who are called out of darkness and who are God's temple. It falls short as a map, because the church does not leave the world physically but separates from what stands under judgment.

study.christ:
The section leads to Christ at several points, and the clearest is the arm of the LORD. The call in 51:9 to the arm to wake, the promise in 52:10 that the LORD has bared His holy arm before the nations, and the question in 53:1, 'to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?', sit in a single run of text. John quotes the question after the crowd refuses to believe Jesus, John 12:38, and Paul quotes it in Romans 10:16. The arm that dried up the sea turns out, in the Gospels, to be a man who is wounded and then raised. The nations are to see God's salvation, 52:10, and Simeon, holding the child, says exactly that: 'my eyes have seen Your salvation', Luke 2:30 to 32.

The herald's cry, 'Your God reigns', anticipates the opening of the Gospels. Jesus comes into Galilee proclaiming the gospel of God and saying the kingdom is near, Mark 1:14 and 15. The word 'gospel' in Greek is the noun built on the same family of words that the Septuagint uses for the herald's good news. Paul connects the herald to the preacher in Romans 10:15, and he links that preaching to the person: those who hear are hearing Christ. Jesus is both the herald and the news.

The promise of comfort for Zion fits Luke's picture of the 'consolation of Israel', for which Simeon was waiting, Luke 2:25. The law that goes out and the justice that becomes a 'light to the nations' in 51:4, with the arms that bring justice in 51:5, are taken up in His ministry and in the apostolic mission, Acts 13:47.

Most striking is the cup. Jerusalem has drained the cup of God's fury and the LORD takes it from her hand. If we read only this chapter, we would see a simple handing over to Babylon. But when we read on to Isaiah 53 and the Gospels, we find that the LORD's hand does not merely remove the cup, it places it into the hands of the Servant. In Gethsemane Jesus asks that it pass, and then accepts it, Matthew 26:39, and He later says He must drink what the Father has given Him, John 18:11. That reading is not forced on the passage but follows from the next chapter, where the Servant is crushed for our iniquities. The cup is lifted from Jerusalem's hand because it is placed in His.

Finally the end of the section sets the pattern of the Messiah's work. The LORD goes before His people and is their rear guard. Christ calls Himself the shepherd who goes ahead of His sheep, John 10:4, and promises that no one can snatch them from His hand, John 10:28. The care that the exiles needed on the road home is the care that believers have on the road to the new creation.

The caution here is to keep the chapter's own emphasis. Its main concern is a literal return, and the Christological readings are drawn from the way the New Testament uses the passage and from its place beside Isaiah 53. We should not say that Abraham or the quarry are hidden pictures of Jesus.
study.god:
The section presents God as the one who makes the first move. He calls Abraham when there was no one, He comforts when no one else can, and He sends His herald before anyone has asked. The people's prayer in 51:9 is real, but the answer in 51:12 begins before they finish speaking: 'I, even I, am He who comforts you.' The comforter is the same God who sent the exile. His anger and His comfort come from the same hand, and He does not hide that.

He is the Maker and the Lord of the heavens. The one who 'stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth', 51:13, is the one who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar, 51:15, and whose name is the LORD of Hosts. The poem sets this large picture beside a very small one, the shadow of His hand over a people He has called by name, 51:16. The God who is too great to be measured is nevertheless near enough to cover them.

He is faithful to His own name. Isaiah 52:5 says that His name is blasphemed all day long among the nations because His people are in captivity, and 52:6 says that for that reason His people will know His name. God treats the honour of His name as bound up with the fate of His people. That is why His salvation has a public edge: 'all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God', 52:10. God does not rescue in secret.

He is just. The cup of fury is real, the wrath was real and the staggering, famished state of Jerusalem in 51:17 to 20 is described without softening. God does not dismiss sin. Yet He is also the one who takes the cup away, who defends His people, 51:22, and who says that their redemption costs them nothing, 52:3. The tension is held by the claim that He gives Himself in the process. The arm that does the saving is His own arm, and the cup removed from His people is placed into the hands of those who tormented them, as an act of justice.

He is the God who goes before and behind. The promise in 52:12 shows the same God who led Israel in a pillar of cloud and fire. They will not need to flee, because the one who leads is also the one who guards the rear.

For worship, the section teaches that confidence is built by remembering what God has done. Praise in this passage is not a mood but a rehearsal of facts: the rock, the sea, the cup, the arm. It also teaches that our fear of men can be broken only by seeing God accurately. The text asks, 'Why should you be afraid of mortal man, of a son of man who withers like grass?' and the answer is to look up at the Maker. Finally, it teaches that the central cry of worship, 'Your God reigns', is something we are sent to announce, not just to feel.

crossReferences.note: The call of Abraham to which Isaiah 51:1 and 2 points. God took one man, promised to make him a great nation and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Isaiah tells exiles to look back to that beginning so that they can believe He will again make something from very little.

Hebrews gives the New Testament comment on Isaiah's Abraham and Sarah. Sarah, barren and beyond the age, conceived because she considered God faithful, and from one man came descendants as numerous as the stars. It shows that Isaiah's call to look to the rock is a call to faith in a promise-keeping God.

The same words as Isaiah 51:11, 'the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing', appear here in Isaiah's earlier vision of the highway of holiness. The repetition ties the two sections together and suggests that the final return, not only the one under Cyrus, is in view.

'By His power He stirred the sea; by His understanding He shattered Rahab.' Job and Isaiah 51:9 draw on the same picture of God overcoming the chaos of the deep. The image tells Isaiah's hearers that no hostile power, whether cosmic or political, has ever stood against Him.

The pillar of cloud that moved behind Israel and stood between them and the Egyptians is the background to the 'rear guard' of Isaiah 52:12. The promise is that the God who guarded His people at the Red Sea will guard them on the road home, so they need not flee in haste.

The LORD hands Jeremiah the cup of the wine of wrath for the nations to drink and stagger. It is the first great use of the image that Isaiah 51:17 to 23 reverses. Jerusalem has drunk, and now the cup goes on to those who tormented her.

'Let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.' Jesus uses the cup language of Isaiah and the prophets for the judgment He is about to bear. The cup that was taken from Jerusalem's hand in Isaiah 51:22 is the one that He consents to drink in her place.

Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7 to show that preachers must be sent, and then quotes Isaiah 53:1 to show that not all welcomed the news. He reads Isaiah's herald as the gospel messenger and the bared arm as the person of Christ, and he sees the unbelief of Israel in the question that follows.

Paul quotes the command of Isaiah 52:11, 'Touch no unclean thing', and gives it to the church. The call to leave Babylon becomes a call to holiness for the people of God who are His temple. The promise attached, 'I will receive you', carries the sense of 52:12 that the LORD goes before them.

'Come out of her, My people.' John hears the departing call of Isaiah 52:11 and Jeremiah 51:6 again at the fall of the final Babylon. The exile and its end have become the pattern for the whole church's relation to a world under judgment.

Simeon holds the infant Jesus and says that his eyes have seen God's salvation, prepared in the sight of all peoples, a light for the Gentiles. He is picking up Isaiah 52:10 and 51:4 and 5 together, and he makes plain that the arm bared before the nations is now present in a child.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 51:1 to 52:12 retells the whole Bible in miniature, and it does so by looking back at each of its great moments. It begins with Abraham, where the story of redemption begins, then goes to creation, when God cut Rahab down and stretched out the heavens. It goes to the exodus, when He made a road in the sea. It reaches the exile, where the story looks broken. And it leaps forward to the end, when the redeemed return with singing and sorrow flees. The passage places the exiles inside the same story and tells them that the God of the first creation and the first exodus is the God of their rescue.

The Eden language of 51:3 matters here. Genesis 2 and 3 ended with a man and woman driven from a garden, and the cherubim at its gate. In Isaiah's vision the wilderness becomes 'like Eden', and the 'garden of the LORD' returns. The sorrow that came into the world in Genesis 3 is the sorrow that 51:11 says will flee. This is the first point where the prophets begin to describe the undoing of the fall, and the New Testament picks it up when it describes the river and the tree of life in the city of God, Revelation 22:1 and 2.

The passage also keeps in view the nations. The law that goes out and the justice that is a light to the nations in 51:4 and 5, and the arm that all the nations see in 52:10, look back to Abraham's calling to be a blessing to the whole earth. Israel's rescue is not an end in itself. It is the means by which God displays His salvation to the world, a point that Simeon, Paul and the early church grasped.

The story moves on to Isaiah 52:13 and the Servant who is raised up and highly exalted. The arm bared in 52:10 is revealed in 53:1, and the cup removed from Jerusalem in 51:22 is the cup that the Servant takes. Paul preaches that the news of 52:7 is the news of Christ crucified and risen. The community that results is called out of Babylon in 52:11, just as in Revelation 18:4 the church is called out of the last Babylon.

The story ends where this poem says it will end. The captives return, they enter Zion with singing, and the unclean no longer enter, 52:1. John sees the holy city coming down out of heaven from God, and hears that the dwelling place of God is with man, Revelation 21:2 and 3. The 'Your God reigns' that a runner shouted over the mountains becomes a settled fact, and the God who went before and behind His people now dwells among them.

quiz.q: Why does Isaiah point Israel back to Abraham and Sarah in 51:1-2?

options.text: To show God's proven pattern of multiplying the one into many, grounding hope for a nation reduced to a remnant.
options.note: The rock and quarry image recalls how God made a whole nation from one man.

options.text: To remind Israel that Abraham never sinned.
options.note: The point is God's multiplying power, not Abraham's sinlessness.

options.text: To prove that Israel no longer needs God's help.
options.note: This overreads the appeal to God's proven power; the passage is precisely a call to continued trust in God's help, not independence from it.

options.text: To explain the geography of the promised land.
options.note: The passage is about God's pattern of grace, not geography.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the cup of the LORD's fury in 51:17-23?

options.text: Zion drained it to the dregs in real judgment, and God announces He will remove it and hand it to her tormentors instead.
It is a cup of blessing Zion had refused to drink.
options.note: It is explicitly the cup of wrath and staggering, not blessing.

options.text: It shows that Zion's judgment will never end.
options.note: The passage announces the judgment's end, not its continuation.

options.text: It refers only to a future judgment on Babylon, with no bearing on Zion.
options.note: Babylon does receive judgment, but the cup is first and explicitly removed from Zion's own hand.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament use Isaiah 52:7, how beautiful are the feet?

options.text: Paul quotes it in Romans 10:15 of those who preach the gospel of Christ.
options.note: Paul applies the verse directly to gospel messengers.

options.text: It is quoted about the feet of the twelve apostles only.
options.note: Apostles are certainly included among gospel messengers, but Paul applies the verse broadly to all who preach the gospel, not a closed list of twelve.

options.text: It has no New Testament citation.
It is used to describe the feet washed at the Last Supper.
options.note: That is a different episode, John 13; this verse is about gospel proclamation.

quiz.q: What connects the arm of the LORD in 51:9-10 to the Servant in Isaiah 53?

options.text: Isaiah 52:10's bared arm leads directly into 53:1's question, to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed, identifying the Servant as that arm.
options.note: The two passages are joined in sequence, tying creation and exodus power to the Servant's revelation.

options.text: They are unrelated images from different sections of the book.
options.note: They are deliberately joined across the chapter break.

options.text: The arm refers only to Cyrus, Israel's Persian deliverer.
options.note: Cyrus is a genuine, earlier instrument of God's arm in Isaiah 45, but this specific arm imagery culminates in the Servant of 53:1, not a foreign king.

options.text: The arm symbolizes Israel's own military strength.
options.note: It is explicitly the LORD's arm, His own saving strength, not Israel's.

questions: Israel was told to look back to Abraham, one person God multiplied into a nation. What small, seemingly insignificant beginning in your life might God be planning to multiply?
The cup of God's wrath was real, drained to the dregs, before it was removed. Where do you need to remember that grace does not deny the reality of judgment, it answers it?
The passage repeatedly commands awake, awake to a people numbed by suffering. What is God calling you to wake up to and stop sleeping through?
The herald's feet are called beautiful simply because of the news they carry. Who in your life needs you to carry good news to them this week?

Zion is told to leave Babylon purified, touching no unclean thing, yet not fleeing in haste, for the LORD goes before and behind. How does knowing God surrounds your obedience change how you leave behind what has held you captive?

translationNotes.note: Rahab here is a poetic name for chaotic sea-power, sometimes read as a cipher for Egypt, not the Rahab of Jericho in Joshua 2, a different word in Hebrew.
